family_history: No family history of aneurysm or SAH

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset severe headache this morning, vomiting, neck stiffness
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Chen is a 48-year-old Asian female with a history of hypertension presenting to the emergency department with a sudden onset severe headache that began approximately 6 hours prior to arrival. She reports she was preparing breakfast when she developed an instantaneous, explosive headache she rates as 10/10 in severity, unlike any headache she has experienced before. She vomited twice before her husband brought her to the emergency department. She denies any preceding warning headache or sentinel event. She reports photophobia and phonophobia since onset. She initially attributed it to stress but her husband noticed she seemed confused briefly right after the onset, though she appears cognitively intact now on arrival. She reports mild ongoing neck pain and stiffness. She denies focal weakness, visual changes, speech difficulties, or loss of consciousness. She has no personal history of migraines or recurrent headaches. Her blood pressure has been controlled on her current regimen per her last primary care visit 2 months ago. She denies any recent trauma, recent illness, or new medications. She reports no exertion or Valsalva maneuver at the time of onset - it came on spontaneously at rest.

output.query: Subarachnoid hemorrhage vasospasm prevention nimodipine outcome

results.finding: Nimodipine 60 mg q4h x21 days reduces poor neurological outcome by 34%
Class I recommendation for oral nimodipine; triple-H therapy for symptomatic vasospasm
Simvastatin did not reduce vasospasm or improve outcomes in SAH

output.summary: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days reduces poor neurological outcome in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (Level I evidence, multiple RCTs). TCD is used for serial vasospasm surveillance; CT perfusion provides objective assessment of cerebral hemodynamics. Intra-arterial therapies (verapamil, balloon angioplasty) have been reported for severe or refractory vasospasm.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from anterior communicating artery aneurysm (Hunt-Hess 2, Fisher 3)

differential.key_features: Thunderclap onset overlaps with SAH; segmental arterial beading on CTA absent in this case
Sudden severe headache and/or neck pain; CTA head and neck without dissection findings
Sudden severe headache with visual changes possible; pituitary MRI / CT without sellar enlargement excludes
Headache subtype overlap; CT venogram or MR venography indicated if SAH excluded
Diagnosis of exclusion; positive CT / CSF xanthochromia rules out for this presentation

optimal_actions.action: Obtain urgent non-contrast CT head as first imaging modality for suspected SAH
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hyperdense blood in subarachnoid spaces (basal cisterns, Sylvian or interhemispheric fissures); CT sensitivity ~98% within 6 h, declines thereafter

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CT angiography (CTA) of the head and neck to characterize aneurysm location, size, and morphology
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Saccular aneurysm at the culprit location; morphologic features (neck width, dome-to-neck ratio, lobulation) inform clipping vs coiling

optimal_actions.action: Interpret labs: CBC, BMP (sodium for cerebral salt wasting / SIADH), coagulation panel, type & screen, troponin, BNP
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis (stress response), troponin elevation (neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy), normal coagulation if not on anticoagulation

optimal_actions.action: Obtain 12-lead ECG to evaluate for neurogenic stress changes and exclude concurrent primary cardiac event
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurogenic T-wave inversions, QTc prolongation, ST changes typical of catecholamine surge in SAH; not primary ACS

optimal_actions.action: Search medical literature for current SAH grading scales (Hunt-Hess, WFNS, modified Fisher) and clipping vs endovascular coiling indications
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Society guidelines (AHA/ASA 2012/2023) confirm grading, vasospasm prophylaxis with nimodipine, and timing of definitive aneurysm securing

tool_parameters.query: aneurysmal SAH management Hunt-Hess WFNS Fisher coiling clipping

optimal_actions.action: Urgent consultation with neurosurgery and interventional neuroradiology for definitive aneurysm securing within 24-72 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Joint decision for endovascular coiling versus surgical clipping based on aneurysm morphology, location, and patient factors

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for nimodipine and any pre-existing antithrombotic / antihypertensive regimen; plan anticoagulation reversal if applicable
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Nimodipine well-tolerated with most antihypertensives (monitor for hypotension); anticoagulation reversed if patient is on a DOAC or warfarin pre-securing aneurysm

optimal_actions.action: Initiate continuous cardiac telemetry for early detection of arrhythmias and neurogenic cardiac complications
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus rhythm with intermittent neurogenic changes; rare malignant arrhythmias warrant intervention

optimal_actions.action: Obtain transthoracic echocardiogram given troponin elevation and neurogenic ECG changes
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Apical ballooning / regional wall motion abnormality consistent with neurogenic (Takotsubo) stress cardiomyopathy; not primary ACS

optimal_actions.action: Initiate daily transcranial Doppler monitoring days 4-14 post-bleed for vasospasm surveillance
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mean flow velocities and Lindegaard ratios to detect cerebral vasospasm preceding delayed cerebral ischemia

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is not part of standard SAH workup; reserve for evaluation of unexplained altered mental status suggesting non-convulsive status epilepticus.
EMG/NCS has no role in acute SAH evaluation or management.
Sleep study is irrelevant to acute SAH workup.
Amyloid PET evaluates Alzheimer biomarkers and has no role in acute hemorrhagic stroke workup.
Dopamine-transporter SPECT is for parkinsonism differentiation and has no role in SAH.
FDG PET has no role in acute SAH diagnosis or management.

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture in SAH with hydrocephalus or intraventricular extension risks transtentorial / tonsillar herniation; CT already confirms SAH so LP is unnecessary and unsafe.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast CT must precede lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect, hydrocephalus, and to confirm/exclude SAH before invasive LP.
Neurosurgical / interventional neuroradiology consultation precedes definitive aneurysm securing within 24-72 hours; medication planning (nimodipine, anticoagulant reversal) aligns with this window.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR/PTT) must be reviewed and any coagulopathy corrected before invasive procedures including lumbar puncture or aneurysm intervention.

critical_actions: Initiate non-contrast CT head as the first diagnostic step in suspected SAH; do not delay for other workup.
Obtain CT angiography of the head and neck immediately after positive non-contrast CT to characterize the aneurysm.
Start nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours within hours of SAH confirmation and continue for 21 days for vasospasm prophylaxis.
Obtain urgent neurosurgery and interventional neuroradiology consultation for definitive aneurysm securing (clipping or coiling) within 24-72 hours.
Admit to a neurocritical care unit with continuous neurologic checks, blood-pressure control (SBP target generally <160 mmHg pre-securing), and cardiac telemetry.
Monitor serum sodium closely for cerebral salt wasting / SIADH and avoid hypotonic fluids.
Initiate daily transcranial Doppler monitoring days 4-14 post-bleed for vasospasm surveillance.
Consult neurosurgery for emergent external ventricular drain placement given acute hydrocephalus.
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture before non-contrast CT in suspected SAH.
Do not perform lumbar puncture when CT already confirms SAH with mass effect, intraventricular hemorrhage, or hydrocephalus — herniation risk.
Do not start aspirin or other antiplatelet agents before the aneurysm is secured — increases rebleeding risk.
Do not administer nimodipine intravenously — IV administration has caused fatal cardiovascular collapse; oral or NG only.
Do not give NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, ketorolac) for headache control before aneurysm securing — antiplatelet effect raises rebleeding risk.
Do not pursue cardiac catheterization for neurogenic troponin elevation without strong primary-ACS evidence — delays aneurysm treatment.
Do not allow uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >160 mmHg) pre-securing; do not over-correct to systemic hypotension.
key_reasoning_points: Sudden, peak-in-seconds 'thunderclap' headache is SAH until proven otherwise — peak intensity ≤1 minute is the highest-yield historical feature.

Non-contrast CT sensitivity for SAH is ~98% within 6 hours of symptom onset, declining to ~80-85% by 24 hours and substantially lower thereafter; CT negativity does not exclude SAH in late presenters.
Lumbar puncture is indicated when CT is non-diagnostic and clinical suspicion remains; xanthochromia by spectrophotometry develops 6-12 hours post-bleed and persists 2-3 weeks.
Distinguish SAH from traumatic LP using non-clearing RBC counts across tubes 1-4 and xanthochromia (absent in traumatic).
Once SAH is confirmed, CT angiography of the head and neck characterizes the aneurysm and drives the clipping-versus-coiling decision.
Hunt-Hess and WFNS grades stratify clinical severity and outcome; modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm risk from CT blood distribution.
Neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo pattern, troponin elevation, T-wave inversions, QTc prolongation) is common in SAH and should not divert attention to a primary cardiac workup.

Nimodipine 60 mg PO every 4 hours for 21 days is the only proven pharmacologic prophylaxis for delayed cerebral ischemia in aneurysmal SAH — it does not prevent angiographic vasospasm but improves outcomes.
Definitive aneurysm securing (coiling or clipping) within 24-72 hours dramatically reduces rebleeding risk, which carries ~50% mortality.
Vasospasm peaks days 4-14 post-bleed; daily transcranial Doppler monitoring plus clinical exam guides escalation to CT perfusion, angiography, and intra-arterial therapy when needed.
Sentinel headache (a milder severe headache hours-to-weeks before a major bleed) is reported in ~10-40% of SAH patients and is a missed opportunity if attributed to migraine.

red_herrings.data_point: Troponin elevation with neurogenic ECG changes (T-wave inversions and QTc prolongation)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Cardiac biomarker rise plus ST/T-wave changes may anchor the workup toward a primary acute coronary syndrome and a cardiology-first pathway.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Catecholamine surge from acute SAH causes neurogenic myocardial injury (Takotsubo physiology) in up to 30-40% of patients; echocardiogram showing apical ballooning confirms etiology and the focus remains on aneurysm securing.

red_herrings.data_point: Past history of migraines, chronic headaches, or fibromyalgia framing the current event as a familiar pattern
red_herrings.intended_effect: Prior headache history can lead to anchoring on a primary headache disorder and under-weighting the abrupt 'worst-ever' character of the current event.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Peak-in-seconds, qualitatively different headache in a known migraineur is still SAH until excluded — the prior diagnosis raises rather than lowers risk if it changes character.

red_herrings.data_point: Bloody CSF in tube 1 raising the possibility of a traumatic tap
red_herrings.intended_effect: A traumatic tap can mimic SAH and falsely reassure if the clinician interprets the blood as procedural.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-clearing RBCs across tubes 1-4 plus xanthochromia on spectrophotometry confirm SAH; traumatic taps show clearing across tubes and lack xanthochromia within the first ~6-12 h.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Multiple co-existing complications (e.g., anticoagulation + hydrocephalus, or sentinel-bleed framing + age) require synthesis across imaging, labs, coagulation reversal, and neurosurgical planning; ≥3 red herrings.
